title: Substantially All Rule
description: The substantially all rule under IRC Section 41 sets an 80% threshold for U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit.
summary: The substantially all rule under IRC Section 41 sets an 80% threshold for U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit. For employee wages, meeting it lets 100% of wages count as qualified research expenses; for business components, at least 80% of research activities must be process of experimentation, or the whole component fails absent shrinking back.

body.text: The substantially all rule under IRC Section 41 sets an 80% threshold for U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit. For employee wages, meeting it lets 100% of wages count as qualified research expenses; for business components, at least 80% of research activities must be process of experimentation, or the whole component fails absent shrinking back.

The "Substantially All" Rule (SAR) is a foundational quantitative gateway within the United States federal Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit regime under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41), establishing an explicit regulatory threshold of at least 80 percent (≥80%). Across the Section 41 framework, the 80% threshold governs two legally and computationally independent determinations that must never be conflated: (1) the Wage Substantially All Rule under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), which determines whether 100% of an individual employee's annual wages qualify as in-house Qualified Research Expenses (QREs), and (2) the Business Component Substantially All Rule under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), which determines whether a defined project or product qualifies as "qualified research" in the first instance by requiring that ≥80% of its research activities constitute elements of a Process of Experimentation (PoE) for a qualified purpose. While meeting the 80% threshold under either rule triggers a 100% inclusion benefit, failing the threshold produces sharply divergent legal consequences: a sub-80% employee wage ratio defaults to a pro-rata wage allocation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1), whereas a sub-80% business component PoE ratio disqualifies the entire business component unless the taxpayer can isolate a qualifying subcomponent under the Shrinking-Back Rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)).

A rigorous examination of the Internal Revenue Code, Treasury Regulations, Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Audit Techniques Guides (ATGs), and recent federal appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence highlights four critical legal distinctions and statutory updates governing the Substantially All Rule:

items: Strict Separation of the Two Regulatory Citations and Fallback Rules: Tax compliance analyses must strictly distinguish the employee wage allocation rules under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2) from the business component Process of Experimentation rules under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) and (b)(2). Specifically, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) governs only whether ≥80% of a business component's research activities constitute elements of a Process of Experimentation; it does not authorize claiming a pro-rata fraction of expenses when a business component falls below 80%. Conversely, claiming a pro-rata percentage (such as 60%) of an individual employee's annual salary when their qualified services fall below 80% is governed by the general wage allocation rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1), not by the Shrinking-Back Rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2), which applies exclusively to narrowing the scope of a business component.

Proper Attribution of Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner: In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit did not alter or newly establish the inclusion of direct supervision and direct support in the numerator of the employee wage SAR under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2). Direct supervision and direct support hours were already explicitly included in the wage SAR numerator by the plain statutory and regulatory text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) whenever an underlying qualified research project exists. Rather, the dispute and appellate holding in Little Sandy Coal addressed the business component (Process of Experimentation) SAR under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), reversing the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of direct supervision, direct support, and pilot-model production activities from the PoE numerator.

Procedural Posture and Holding of Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner: In Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 11019-19 (U.S. Tax Court, Order issued March 14, 2024; related order May 30, 2024), the IRS aggressively challenged a custom electrical equipment manufacturer's pilot-model claims under the business component SAR of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6). However, the Tax Court's March 14, 2024 order denied the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment, clarifying that Little Sandy Coal does not categorically bar pilot-model production expenses (26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(4)) as a matter of law from the numerator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction, provided the taxpayer substantiates at trial that those fabrication activities constituted elements of a Process of Experimentation.

Statutory Enactment of IRC Section 174A under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA): On July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Section 70302), creating 26 U.S.C. § 174A to permanently restore immediate expensing for domestic research or experimental expenditures for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, and amending 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to require that expenditures "are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A". While 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) and (a)(6) (last amended via T.D. 10024 on January 15, 2025) and pre-2025 judicial opinions continue to reference Section 174, post-2024 compliance for the remaining ≤20% of non-PoE research activities under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) is governed statutorily by Section 174A.

body.text: Dual Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Substantially All Rule

Within IRC Section 41, the phrase "substantially all" appears in two distinct statutory subsections that operate at separate stages of the R&D tax credit determination. As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide on Qualified Research Expenses (last updated July 2, 2026) explicitly instructs examiners, "The 'substantially all' for wages differs from the 'substantially all rule' for Process of Experimentation". Reinforcing this separation, Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) mandates that the business component Process of Experimentation 80% test be computed "without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2)" (the employee wage 80% safe harbor). Consequently, a taxpayer cannot use the fact that an engineer's wages were grossed up from 80% to 100% under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) to alter the proportion of Process of Experimentation activities in the business component calculation under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), nor does passing the business component 80% test automatically qualify 100% of the wages of an employee who spent less than 80% of their annual service hours on qualified services.

body.text: Analysis of Dual Enforcement Dynamics

Taxpayers and practitioners historically treated both 80% thresholds primarily as credit-optimization mechanisms—enabling the full inclusion of senior technical personnel compensation when non-R&D administrative duties remained at or below 20%, and absorbing up to 20% of non-experimental support activities within qualifying R&D projects. In the current examination and litigation environment, however, the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) Division and Small Business/Self-Employed (SB/SE) examiners actively deploy the Business Component Substantially All Rule under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as an all-or-nothing audit threshold to disqualify entire projects when routine production, commercial integration, or unsubstantiated supervisory hours dilute the Process of Experimentation ratio below 80%. Simultaneously, examiners scrutinize C-suite and upper-level engineering management wages under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2) and (d), disallowing both the 80% safe harbor and underlying pro-rata claims where taxpayers fail to separate first-line supervision of experimentation from general executive oversight.
The Substantially All Rule for Employee Wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d))
Statutory and Regulatory Mechanics of Qualified Services

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1), a taxpayer's "qualified research expenses" (QREs) equal the sum of in-house research expenses and contract research expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on a trade or business. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), "in-house research expenses" comprise three statutory categories: (i) any "wages" paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee; (ii) any amount paid or incurred for "supplies" (defined in § 41(b)(2)(C) as tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and depreciable property) used in the conduct of qualified research; and (iii) under regulations, amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research.

For Section 41 purposes, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i) defines "wages" by cross-reference to 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a), encompassing all taxable employee compensation subject to federal income tax withholding as reported on Form W-2, including regular salaries, bonuses, and taxable stock option redemptions. As clarified in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide on Qualified Research Expenses (updated July 2, 2026), when an employee exercises stock options and the spread is included in wages subject to withholding, whether those option wages constitute QREs in the exercise year depends on whether the services performed by the employee in the grant year constituted qualified services. For self-employed individuals and owner-employees within the meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 401(c)(1), "wages" include earned income as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 401(c)(2). By contrast, nontaxable fringe benefits not subject to withholding (such as pre-tax 401(k) contributions or nontaxable health insurance benefits) and any wages taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Credit under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a) (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii)) are strictly excluded from Section 41 wages, even if paid to a full-time research scientist.
Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), "qualified services" are restricted to three specific categories of employee activity:

items: Engaging in Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)): The term "engaging in qualified research" means the actual, hands-on conduct of qualified research—as in the case of a scientist conducting laboratory experiments, an engineer formulating and testing physical prototypes, or a computer scientist writing and evaluating experimental algorithms. In specialized contexts, the IRS Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit Audit Guidelines note that a laboratory employee responsible for day-to-day mentoring or guiding of the laboratory research of others is treated as "actually engaged in qualified research" rather than performing supervision.

Direct Supervision of Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)): The term "direct supervision" means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research—as in the case of a research scientist or engineering lead who directly supervises laboratory experiments, even if that supervisor does not personally perform the physical experiments. Crucially, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2) enforces a strict "one-up" boundary: "'Direct supervision' does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist". In Scott Moore and Gayla Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (Dkt. No. 18632-19, Feb. 23, 2023), aff'd (7th Cir. 2024), the taxpayers owned an S corporation (Nevco, Inc.) that manufactured sports-venue scoreboards and video displays and claimed 65% of President and Chief Operating Officer (COO) Gary Robert's base compensation ($85,092 in 2014 and $178,956 in 2015, plus bonuses) as wage QREs. Although the IRS conceded that the wages of Nevco's engineers and its Director of Engineering (Dave Paslay) qualified across five development projects (Scoreboard Truss, Scorbitz, New Caney Ribbon Board, MPCX-2, and Slim Shot Clock), the Tax Court disallowed 100% of the claimed 65% allocation for the COO. Because the engineers reported to the Director of Engineering, who in turn reported to the COO, the COO was two management layers removed from the researchers—constituting non-qualified "supervision of supervision" under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)—and the taxpayers lacked contemporaneous task-specific records distinguishing any hands-on experimental work by the COO from general "new product development" management.

Direct Support of Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)): The term "direct support" means services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3), qualifying direct support includes the services of a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research data, and a machinist machining a part of an experimental model used in qualified research. Conversely, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) explicitly excludes general and administrative (G&A) services or services only indirectly of benefit to research activities—such as payroll personnel preparing salary checks for laboratory scientists, an accountant accounting for research expenses, a janitor performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, or corporate officers engaged in supervising financial, budgeting, inventory, or personnel matters—regardless of whether those G&A personnel are part of the research department or in a separate department. Furthermore, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3) specifies that "[d]irect support does not include supervision," meaning upper-tier managers cannot recharacterize multi-layer oversight as "direct support" to circumvent the first-line limitation of paragraph (c)(2).

body.text: Computational Fraction and the Exclusion of Non-Service Time

Under the general allocation rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1), wages paid to or incurred for an employee constitute in-house research expenses only to the extent they were paid or incurred for qualified services performed by the employee. When an employee performs both qualified services and nonqualified services during a taxable year, in the absence of another allocation method that the taxpayer can demonstrate to be more appropriate, the amount of in-house wage QREs is determined by multiplying the employee's total annual taxable wages by the ratio of total time actually spent performing qualified services to total time spent performing all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year:

Under the "Substantially All" rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), if the wages allocated on this time-ratio basis to services meeting the requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) (engaging in qualified research) or (ii) (direct supervision or direct support of qualified research) constitute at least 80 percent (≥80%) of the wages paid to or incurred by the taxpayer for the employee during the taxable year, then "the term 'qualified services' means all of the services performed by the employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year". Consequently, meeting the ≥80% threshold allows 100% of the employee's annual § 3401(a) wages to be claimed as in-house wage QREs, absorbing up to 20% of non-qualified work time. If the employee's ratio is less than 80% (<80%), the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) safe harbor does not apply, and the taxpayer is limited to claiming the actual pro-rata percentage of wages attributable to qualified services under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1).

A critical computational rule verified in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide on Qualified Research Expenses (last updated July 2, 2026) governs the treatment of paid leave: non-service time—specifically sick leave (as well as analogous vacation and paid time off during which no services are performed)—is excluded from both the numerator and the denominator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d) fraction. Because 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1) defines the denominator strictly as "the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year," paid leave does not dilute an employee's qualified service ratio, while the resulting percentage (or 100% if ≥80%) is applied against the employee's total annual W-2 Box 1 wages (which include paid leave compensation).

body.text: Scope of Little Sandy Coal vs. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)

In analyzing the inclusion of direct supervision and direct support within the Substantially All Rule, it is essential not to confuse the Seventh Circuit's holding in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, with the employee wage SAR under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2). Under the plain text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), the employee wage SAR has always provided that "if substantially all of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of services meeting the requirements of section 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii), then the term 'qualified services' means all of the services performed by the employee". Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) explicitly defines qualified services to include "engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities which constitute qualified research," an employee's direct supervision and direct support hours have always been included in the numerator of that employee's wage fraction under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), provided an underlying "qualified research" business component exists under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d).

Rather, the legal controversy in Little Sandy Coal centered on the Business Component (Process of Experimentation) Substantially All Rule under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6). In its memorandum opinion (T.C. Memo. 2021-15), the Tax Court drew a rigid boundary between 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) ("engaging in qualified research") and § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) ("direct supervision or direct support"), holding that employees providing direct supervision or direct support—such as production employees fabricating hull structures for a prototype vessel—are not themselves "engaged in" research and therefore their activities cannot be included in the numerator of the business component 80% Process of Experimentation fraction under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6). On appeal (62 F.4th 287), the Seventh Circuit rejected that categorical exclusion from the business component PoE test, holding that direct supervision, direct support, and pilot-model production activities must be included in both the numerator and the denominator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) business component fraction if their costs qualify as research expenses under Section 174 (now Section 174A for domestic post-2024 expenditures) and the activities constitute elements of a Process of Experimentation.
Hypothetical Worked Examples: Wage Substantially All Rule and the 79% vs. 80% Cliff Effect
The following three numerical scenarios demonstrate the exact arithmetic operation of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2) and the financial impact of tracking first-line supervision and support hours:

items: Hypothetical Example 1 — Supervisory Engineer Combining Hands-On Research and First-Line Supervision: Suppose a senior supervisory engineer earning $150,000 in annual § 3401(a) wages dedicates 70% of their total annual service hours (excluding sick leave and vacation) to hands-on qualified research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)), 15% to immediate first-line direct supervision of engineers conducting qualified research (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)), and 15% to general administrative management and budgeting. Because both hands-on qualified research (70%) and first-line direct supervision (15%) satisfy 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i)–(ii) and enter the numerator of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), the engineer's qualified service ratio is 70% + 15% = 85%. Because 85% meets the ≥80% threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), 100% of the engineer's annual wages ($150,000)—including the $22,500 ($150,000 × 15%) attributable to general administrative duties—qualifies as an in-house wage QRE. Had the taxpayer failed to document the 15% first-line direct supervision separately from general administrative management, the engineer's substantiated ratio would have dropped to 70% (<80%), restricting claimable wage QREs to $105,000 ($150,000 × 70%) under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1)—a reduction of $45,000 in QREs from a single employee.

Hypothetical Example 2 — The One-Percentage-Point Cliff Multiplier (79% vs. 80%): Suppose an employee's contemporaneous time logs substantiate that 79% of their total annual service hours were spent performing qualified services and 21% were spent on non-qualified routine commercial production. Because 79% falls below the 80% threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2), the taxpayer is restricted to the pro-rata allocation rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1) and may claim only 79% of the employee's annual wages. If contemporaneous documentation substantiates just one additional percentage point of qualified service time—bringing the employee's ratio to 80%—26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) triggers 100% wage inclusion. Consequently, falling short of the wage SAR by a single percentage point (79% versus 80%) results in an immediate loss of 21 percentage points (100% − 79% = 21%) of that employee's annual wages from the QRE base.

Hypothetical Example 3 — Pro-Rata Allocation Below 80% (Distinguishing Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) from the Shrinking-Back Rule): Suppose a project manager earning $150,000 in annual taxable wages spends 60% of their annual service hours directly supervising front-line R&D engineers (a qualified service under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)) and 40% on commercial client relations and administrative scheduling. Because 60% is less than 80%, the employee does not qualify for the 100% inclusion safe harbor of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2). Under the general pro-rata wage allocation rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(1) (and not the business-component Shrinking-Back Rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)), the taxpayer claims 60% of the salary ($90,000) as in-house wage QREs and excludes the remaining 40% ($60,000).

body.text: Substantiation Standards for Employee Wages

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) (cross-referencing general record retention rules under 26 U.S.C. § 6001 and 26 C.F.R. § 1.6001-1), a taxpayer claiming a credit under Section 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit". When examining employee wage QREs and testing the 80% threshold under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d), the IRS Audit Techniques Guide on Qualified Research Expenses (last updated July 2, 2026) identifies five primary documentary sources used by revenue agents to establish what duties an employee performed and the hours spent performing them: (1) payroll records (including Forms W-2, payroll registers, and stock-option exercise schedules reconciled to the general ledger); (2) employee job descriptions; (3) performance evaluations; (4) calendars; and (5) appointment books (supplemented by contemporaneous project time-tracking logs, lab notebooks, engineering meeting minutes, and employee interviews).

The IRS ATG emphasizes that eligibility for qualified services is determined solely by what an employee actually does during a specific taxable period, never by job titles, generic job descriptions, or academic/technical degrees. Furthermore, the IRS Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit Audit Guidelines instruct examiners to stratify employees by organizational level: front-line laboratory scientists and immediate first-line section heads (classified as "Box A" and "Box B" personnel located in or near research laboratories) normally spend ≥80% of their time in qualified services and present lower audit risk, whereas personnel above first-line supervision ("Box C" and "Box D" executives and directors) are subjected to intensive activity-level scrutiny requiring corroboration from business calendars, travel records, project reports, laboratory books, and budget responsibility records.

In federal litigation, courts have increasingly restricted taxpayers' ability to rely on the Cohan rule (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)) to estimate employee wage allocations when contemporaneous time records are absent. While earlier decisions such as Fudim v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1994-235, and Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, accepted reconstructed percentage estimates where witnesses possessed deep technical involvement corroborated by patents, scientific publications, or institutional documentation, recent decisions—including Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, aff'd (7th Cir. 2024), and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84—hold that courts will refuse to apply Cohan to estimate wage QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) unless the taxpayer first establishes with credible, objective evidence that qualified research occurred on a specific business component under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) and provides a principled mathematical basis separating experimentation from general product development.
The Substantially All Rule for Business Components (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6))
The Four-Part Test and the Qualified Purpose Requirement

Whereas the employee wage SAR governs the includable proportion of an individual's compensation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), the second—and far more frequently litigated—application of the Substantially All Rule operates at the project level under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) to determine whether research activities constitute "qualified research". Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the qualification tests of Section 41(d)(1) must be applied separately with respect to each discrete business component of the taxpayer. Section 41(d)(2)(B) defines a "business component" as "any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be—(i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer". In addition, under the special production-process rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(1), any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component from the product itself, and research activities relating to the product versus the manufacturing process must each independently satisfy Section 41(d).

For activities with respect to a business component to constitute "qualified research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2), the taxpayer must satisfy all four parts of the statutory Four-Part Test (and not be excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) or § 41(d)(4)):

items: The Section 174A / Section 174 Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i)): The research must be research with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174A (for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, or under 26 U.S.C. § 174 for pre-2025 tax years). Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and are intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a product or process, or the appropriate design of that product or process.

The Discovering Technological Information Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Under final regulations (T.D. 9104, 69 FR 22, Jan. 2, 2004; 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)), there is no requirement that the taxpayer seek to obtain knowledge that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor must the research succeed; rather, the research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component, and it is technological in nature if the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(4)).

The Business Component Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)): The taxpayer must intend that the information to be discovered be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. (Where the business component is Internal Use Software [IUS] developed primarily for the taxpayer's internal general and administrative functions rather than for commercial sale, lease, license, or third-party interaction, the software must also satisfy the three-part High Threshold of Innovation Test under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii): it must be innovative, involve significant economic risk due to substantial technical uncertainty, and be commercially unavailable.)

The Process of Experimentation and "Substantially All" Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Substantially all (≥80%) of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a Process of Experimentation (PoE) that relates to a qualified purpose under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3).

body.text: Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software, a Process of Experimentation is an evaluative process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. Specifically, the taxpayer must establish a three-step evaluative cycle fundamentally relying on hard-science, engineering, or computer-science principles:

items: Identification of technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving the business component;
Identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and

Identification and conduct of a process of evaluating the alternatives (through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology that tests hypotheses and refines or discards alternatives).

body.text: Crucially, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) stipulates that although a taxpayer may undertake a process of experimentation when only the appropriate design is uncertain at the outset (even if capability and method are known), mere uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component—or merely demonstrating that initial uncertainty was eliminated—"does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation".

Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(A) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), a Process of Experimentation is undertaken for a qualified purpose only if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), research is explicitly disqualified from having a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Any research activity directed at aesthetic, cosmetic, or seasonal modifications is excluded from the numerator of the 80% PoE test.
The 80/20 Rule and Statutory Currency: IRC Section 174 vs. IRC Section 174A

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the Substantially All requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(iii) is satisfied "only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in section 41(d)(3)".

When a taxpayer's research activities for a discrete business component meet or exceed this 80% threshold, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) operates as an inclusionary 80/20 rule: the business component satisfies 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) "even if the remaining 20 percent (or less) of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the business component do not constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in section 41(d)(3), so long as these remaining research activities satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under section 41(d)(4)". For example, in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 4, an automotive manufacturer designing a new hood to meet fuel-economy goals conducted modeling, simulation, testing, and refinement across the hood, air intake, and cooling systems that constituted 85% of total project activities, while the remaining 15% consisted of non-evaluative research activities; because 85% ≥ 80%, 100% of the project's research activities satisfied the Substantially All requirement so long as the remaining 15% satisfied Section 41(d)(1)(A) and were not excluded under Section 41(d)(4).

By contrast, activities explicitly excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c) can never be absorbed into the remaining ≤20% bucket. These statutorily excluded activities encompass: (A) research after commercial production (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(2)), defined as activities conducted after the component meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements, including preproduction planning for a finished component, tooling-up for production, trial production runs, troubleshooting faults in production equipment or processes, accumulating production data, and debugging flaws in a business component; (B) adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(3)); (C) duplication of an existing business component in whole or in part from a physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(C); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(4)); (D) efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research, routine data collection, or ordinary quality-control testing and inspection (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(D); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(5)); (F) foreign research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F)); (G) research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(G)); and (H) funded research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity where the taxpayer does not retain substantial rights or does not bear the financial risk of failure (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)).
Statutory Currency Across Three Legislative Eras (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A): Section 174 vs. Section 174A)

When evaluating whether the remaining ≤20% of non-PoE research activities satisfy 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) under the 80/20 rule of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), tax practitioners and auditors must distinguish among three distinct statutory periods:

items: Pre-2022 Tax Years (Historical Section 174 Expensing Regime): For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022—including the tax years litigated in Little Sandy Coal (FYE June 30, 2014), Intermountain Electronics (2012–2015), and Moore (2014–2015)—26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) defined qualified research as research "with respect to which expenditures may be treated as expenses under section 174," which allowed taxpayers to immediately deduct research or experimental expenditures or elect 60-month amortization.

Tax Years 2022–2024 (TCJA Capitalization Regime): Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, P.L. 115-97), effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, through taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025, Congress amended 26 U.S.C. § 174 to eliminate immediate expensing and mandate that "specified research or experimental expenditures" be capitalized and amortized ratably over 5 years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research, while amending 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to reference expenditures that "may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174".

Tax Years Beginning After December 31, 2024 (Current Law under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — IRC § 174A): On July 4, 2025, Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21, Section 70302), effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. The OBBBA enacted IRC Section 174A (26 U.S.C. § 174A), permanently restoring immediate deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures (while leaving foreign R&E expenditures subject to 15-year capitalization and amortization under 26 U.S.C. § 174, providing 1-year or 2-year transition recovery in 2025/2026 for unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E costs, and allowing eligible small businesses meeting the ≤$50 million 3-year average gross receipts test to elect retroactive immediate expensing on amended 2022–2024 returns). Crucially, the OBBBA amended the statutory text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to read: "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A". Practitioners should note two additional technical nuances of the OBBBA amendment: first, the statutory wording shifted from "may be treated as" (under prior Section 174) to "are treated as" (under Section 174A), requiring alignment between a taxpayer's Section 174A domestic R&E treatment (and Section 280C(c) deduction reduction or timely reduced-credit election) and its Section 41 QRE pool; second, Congress did not reinsert the historical statutory "reasonableness" clause into the text of new Section 174A. Although Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) and (a)(6) (last amended via T.D. 10024, 90 FR 4096, Jan. 15, 2025) still contain the unamended regulatory text referencing Section 174, the enacted statute (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A)) controls for all tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.

body.text: Cost-Basis Measurement Controversies and Exclusion of Supply Costs

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the ≥80% Process of Experimentation threshold is measured "on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2))". In examination practice, defending the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) calculation on a cost basis is substantially more complex than defending the hourly employee wage fraction under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d), because taxpayers must establish a documented nexus allocating labor and third-party contract research activities between active Process of Experimentation tasks and non-evaluative tasks at the individual business component level. Two major measurement fallacies have been decisively rejected by the U.S. Tax Court in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (affirmed on appeal, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)).

First, the Tax Court rejected the Physical-Element / Novelty Proportion Method. Relying on the district court decision in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), the taxpayer in Little Sandy Coal argued that its tanker barge project satisfied the 80% Substantially All Rule because the redesigned hull alone made up 90% of the vessel and over 80% of the vessel's physical systems differed from prior vessels. The Tax Court explicitly declined to follow Trinity Industries, holding that 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) requires the 80% test to be applied with respect to research activities, not the physical elements or components of the product being developed. As Judge Halpern explained, the physical proportion of novel elements is not a reasonable basis for measuring research activities because the extent of experimentation does not vary in proportion to physical component size—a small, complex subsystem may require extensive experimentation, whereas a massive structural hull may involve little or no experimentation once designed.

Second, the Tax Court established the Categorical Exclusion of Physical Supply Costs from the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) Fraction. In Little Sandy Coal, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the taxpayer incurred $3,892,142 in supply costs on its Apex Tanker (Project 720) and $1,943,265 in supply costs on its Dry Dock (Project 730). The Tax Court held that because the Substantially All test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) measures activities, physical supplies (defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) as tangible property) are not activities and therefore must be excluded from both the numerator and the denominator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction, even when the taxpayer measures research activities by their cost. In the Tax Court's exact words: "[E]ven when those activities are measured by their cost, the [amount] CIS paid for supplies used in building the dry dock would not be part of the fraction described in [Treas. Reg. S]ection 1.41-4(a)(6)". Only after a business component independently satisfies the ≥80% research activity threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) do supplies used in the conduct of that qualified research become eligible in-house QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).
Strategic Mitigation and Judicial Precedent
The Shrinking-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2))

When an overall business component (such as an entire commercial vessel, a custom industrial assembly, or an enterprise software platform) fails to reach the ≥80% Process of Experimentation threshold under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), 100% of the overall business component is disqualified from the Section 41 credit unless the taxpayer can apply the Shrinking-Back Rule codified in 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2).

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2), the Four-Part Test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2) is applied first at the level of the discrete overall business component (the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business). If all requirements of Section 41(d)(1) (including the ≥80% PoE test) are met at that overall level, the analysis stops and the overall component qualifies. If the overall business component fails to satisfy those requirements—for example, because non-experimental system integration, standard user-interface coding, or commercial hull fabrication pushes Process of Experimentation activities below 80%—then the requirements of Section 41(d)(1) are applied to the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention. This iterative "shrinking back" continues step-by-step to progressively smaller subsets of elements until either:

items: A subset of elements of the business component is reached that independently satisfies all requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) (including the ≥80% Process of Experimentation threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)), or
The most basic element of the business component is reached and fails to satisfy the requirements.

body.text: Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(3) illustrates this mechanism with a motorcycle engine manufacturer (X) that develops a novel carburetor and modifies an existing motorcycle engine design to accommodate it: under the Shrinking-Back Rule, the Section 41(d)(1) tests are applied first to the overall motorcycle engine; if the engine as a whole fails the ≥80% Process of Experimentation test because the engine modifications were minor or routine, the test shrinks back to the next most significant subset of elements—the new carburetor—allowing the research activities in developing the carburetor to qualify independently. (Note also that Treasury Regulation 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(5) contains an analogous shrinking-back rule for determining whether costs qualify as research or experimental expenditures at the component or subcomponent level when uncertainty does not exist for the overall product, though Section 174/174A itself has no 80% Substantially All requirement.)

As 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) explicitly states, the Shrinking-Back Rule is applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy Section 41(d)(1) with respect to the overall business component, and "is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility". However, to invoke 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) in an examination or before the Tax Court when an overall project falls below 80%, the taxpayer bears the affirmative evidentiary burden of maintaining granular, subcomponent-level time and cost accounting; if a taxpayer tracks wages and costs only at the whole-product level, neither the IRS nor a court can compute the 80% PoE fraction for a shrunk-back subcomponent, resulting in total disallowance.

body.text: Judicial Review and Heightened IRS Scrutiny

Federal tax litigation over the past several years demonstrates how the U.S. Tax Court, the U.S. Courts of Appeals, and state tax tribunals enforce the Substantially All Rule and its accompanying substantiation requirements:
1. Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (Feb. 11, 2021), aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. Mar. 7, 2023) (No. 21-3145)

In Little Sandy Coal, the petitioner (headquartered in Lamar, Indiana) filed a consolidated federal income tax return for its fiscal year ended June 30, 2014, claiming $1,141,713 in Section 41 research credits attributable to its shipbuilding subsidiary, Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS), across 11 vessel development projects. The IRS disallowed the entire $1,141,713 credit, determining a tax deficiency of $324,529 and an accuracy-related penalty under IRC Section 6662 of $64,910. By binding stipulation, trial before Judge Halpern focused on representative pilot-model projects, primarily Project 720 (the Apex Tanker)—an 87,000-barrel tank barge built for Apex Oil, Inc. based on a prior barge design (the Penn 80) but featuring a redesigned stern notch, towing bridle, "wind sail" anchor calculations, longitudinal strength calculations, and a vapor barrier coating system, for which CIS claimed $2,505,491 in wages, $17,504 in contract weld-testing expenses paid to Hayes Testing Labs, and $3,892,142 in supply costs—and Project 730 (the Dry Dock)—CIS's first floating dry dock built for Detyens Shipyard, featuring five design revisions to an outboard side plate and an 18-inch raised safety deck, for which CIS claimed $146,109 in wages and $1,943,265 in supply costs. In addition, CIS claimed $609,276 in unallocated, estimated nonproduction engineering and management wages across all projects, including 60% ($173,996) of the total wages of lead naval architect Bud Johnson, $126,734 for executives Don Foertsch, David Foertsch, and Alan Fleischmann, and $56,895 for draftsmen Dennis Gass, Kyle Harpenau, and Robert Kellems.

As noted above, the Tax Court (T.C. Memo. 2021-15) ruled that production employees fabricating the vessels, as well as direct supervision and direct support personnel under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii), were not directly "engaged in" qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and therefore could not be included in the numerator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) 80% Process of Experimentation fraction. On appeal (62 F.4th 287, decided March 7, 2023), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit rejected the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of direct supervision, direct support, and production activities from the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) numerator. The Seventh Circuit held that activities involving direct supervision, direct support, and pilot-model fabrication can constitute elements of a Process of Experimentation and, when they do, their costs must be included in both the numerator and the denominator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction, provided those costs qualify as research expenses under IRC Section 174.

Despite correcting the Tax Court's legal formulation of the numerator, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the complete disallowance of Little Sandy Coal's $1,141,713 credit claim. Rather than maintaining contemporaneous time-tracking or activity logs showing which hours involved evaluating technical alternatives, CIS relied on oral trial testimony, arbitrary nonproduction management wage allocations (such as the unrecorded 60% estimate for its lead engineer), and an engineering technician's post-hoc estimate that 87% of production hours on the Apex Tanker went to parts differing from the Penn 80 (plus 10% to similar items). Rejecting these methods, the Seventh Circuit emphasized (62 F.4th at 308) that "Section 41(d) requires us to walk by sight, not by faith" and that "shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice... [s]omething more, such as documentation of time spent on such activities, is necessary". Furthermore, because CIS adopted an "all-or-nothing" litigation posture—claiming the entire vessels as single business components without accounting records breaking out engineering, supervision, and fabrication costs for specific novel subcomponents such as the stern notch, towing bridle, or outboard side plate—the taxpayer could not invoke the Shrinking-Back Rule under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to salvage partial credits.
2. Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 11019-19 (U.S. Tax Court, Order of March 14, 2024)

In Intermountain Electronics, the petitioner—a Utah-based C corporation that designs, engineers, manufactures, and services custom electrical distribution and control equipment (including specialized switchgears, transformers, controls, and e-houses for underground and surface mining, oil and gas refineries, power generation, and government projects)—claimed Section 41 R&D tax credits for tax years 2012 through 2015. Intermountain Electronics treated each custom, nonrepeatable electrical equipment assembly as a "pilot model" under 26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(4) (which defines a pilot model as "any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product") and claimed QREs for nonproduction engineers, production fabrication/assembly employees, and supplies.

The IRS disallowed the credits and moved for partial summary judgment, relying on the Tax Court's earlier opinion in Little Sandy Coal (T.C. Memo. 2021-15) to argue that production expenses incurred in manufacturing custom pilot models are categorically excluded from the numerator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) 80% Process of Experimentation fraction—which would make it mathematically impossible for Intermountain's pilot models to reach the ≥80% threshold. In an Order issued March 14, 2024 (followed by a related order on May 30, 2024, Judge Ronald L. Buch), the Tax Court denied the IRS's motion for partial summary judgment. Aligning its jurisprudence with the Seventh Circuit's appellate ruling in Little Sandy Coal, the Tax Court held that precedent does not foreclose pilot-model production expenses from being included in the numerator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction as a matter of law. Instead, whether production costs enter the PoE numerator is a question of material fact for trial, where the taxpayer bears the burden of proving through detailed activity analysis, cost accounting, and contemporaneous documentation that specific physical fabrication activities constituted elements of a Process of Experimentation.
3. Scott Moore, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (Feb. 23, 2023), aff'd (7th Cir. 2024), and Related Substantiation Decisions

Complementing Little Sandy Coal and Intermountain Electronics, the Tax Court and Seventh Circuit decisions in Scott Moore and Gayla Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (Dkt. No. 18632-19, Judge Colvin), aff'd (7th Cir. 2024), together with Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and state administrative rulings such as California Office of Tax Appeals Opinion In the Matter of the Appeal of Abramson (2024-OTA-636) and Idaho State Tax Commission Decision No. 2-117-100-544, reinforce three strict evidentiary standards across both branches of the Substantially All Rule. First, under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2), upper-level executives who supervise first-line engineering managers ("two layers removed") are barred as a matter of law from claiming "direct supervision," and general product-development oversight cannot be claimed without task-level time records isolating hands-on experimentation. Second, taxpayers cannot satisfy the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) 80% PoE test merely by asserting that they "only claimed qualified hours" (which circularly yields a 100% ratio) or by submitting vague timesheet descriptions such as "design meeting" or "team meeting to review drawings" (Abramson, 2024-OTA-636). Third, unrecorded conversational inquiries or experience-based percentage estimates (such as 60%–65% executive allocations) will not sustain either the 80% wage safe harbor or pro-rata QRE allocations on audit.

body.text: Integrated Practical Application and Compliance Strategy
Hypothetical Worked Example: Dual Application of the Substantially All Rule

To illustrate how both branches of the Substantially All Rule interact sequentially within a single R&D tax credit computation, consider a technology company developing a proprietary industrial sensor system.

In Step 1 (Business Component SAR Evaluation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), and § 1.41-4(b)(2)), the company initially evaluates the entire proprietary sensor system as a single overarching business component under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B). Project cost-accounting records measuring research activities by cost (strictly excluding physical supply costs per Little Sandy Coal, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, and computing employee costs without regard to the wage 80% gross-up per 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)) reveal that 75% of the total research activities for the overall sensor system constituted elements of a Process of Experimentation (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)), while the remaining 25% consisted of routine commercial system integration testing that did not evaluate technical alternatives. Because 75% is less than the ≥80% threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the overall sensor system fails the Business Component Substantially All Rule, meaning 0% of the project's expenditures would qualify if claimed at the whole-system level. However, because the company maintained subcomponent-level project accounting, it applies the Shrinking-Back Rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)) to narrow the business component definition to the discrete chemical compound formulation and sensing-element subsystem. Within this narrowed subcomponent, 95% of the research activity costs involved a systematic Process of Experimentation (identifying material sensitivity uncertainty and evaluating alternative chemical formulations via laboratory trials), and the remaining 5% involved baseline domestic research support activities satisfying 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) (domestic research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174A for post-2024 tax years, or § 174 for pre-2025 tax years) and not excluded under § 41(d)(4). Because 95% meets the ≥80% threshold of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the shrunk-back chemical formulation subcomponent passes the Business Component SAR, and under the 80/20 absorption rule, 100% (95% + 5% = 100%) of the eligible research activities for that chemical formulation subcomponent constitute qualified research.

In Step 2 (Wage SAR Evaluation under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2)), once the shrunk-back chemical compound formulation subcomponent is established as qualified research under Step 1, the company evaluates the annual service hours of its lead materials scientist assigned to that subcomponent. Contemporaneous time logs show that during the taxable year, the scientist spent 84% of their total annual service hours (excluding sick leave and paid vacation) formulating, modeling, and testing alternative chemical compounds for the sensing element (hands-on qualified research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(1)), and the remaining 16% (100% − 84% = 16%) on general administrative reporting and non-R&D department meetings. Because the scientist's qualified service ratio for the taxable year is 84%—which meets the ≥80% threshold of the Wage Substantially All Rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2))—the company properly claims 100% of the lead materials scientist's annual § 3401(a) taxable W-2 wages as in-house wage QREs.
Actionable Compliance and Audit-Defense Protocols

To substantiate both branches of the Substantially All Rule and withstand IRS examination under current statutory, regulatory, and Form 6765 reporting standards, tax departments and R&D credit advisors should implement four structural compliance protocols:

items: Deploy Dual-Tagging in Contemporaneous Time and Cost Accounting Systems Aligned with Mandatory Form 6765 Section G Reporting: Because the IRS evaluates the Wage SAR (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)) on an employee-by-employee hourly basis and the Business Component SAR (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)) on a component-by-component activity/cost basis, aggregate departmental R&D hour tracking is legally inadequate. Moreover, under the finalized IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, released February 2026), Section G (Business Component Information)—which was optional for tax years beginning before 2026—becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 (starting with the 2026 tax year) for all filers except (a) qualified small businesses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h)(3) that elect the payroll tax credit offset on Form 6765, and (b) original-return filers with controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less and prior 3-year average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less under 26 U.S.C. § 448(c)(3). Note that Section G introduces a third, purely administrative "80%/Top 50" reporting rule requiring non-exempt taxpayers to itemize business components in descending order of QREs until accounting for at least 80% of total QREs (up to a maximum of 50 business components, with remaining components reported under "Aggregate Business Components"), breaking out direct research, direct supervision, and direct support wages plus supplies, computer leasing, and contract research across columns 49–56. To support both the substantive SAR thresholds and Section G disclosure, enterprise time-tracking and ERP systems must simultaneously tag hours by: (a) Employee Service Category (Hands-On Research [§ 1.41-2(c)(1)], First-Line Direct Supervision [§ 1.41-2(c)(2)], Direct Support [§ 1.41-2(c)(3)], Non-Qualified Service, or Excluded Non-Service Leave for the § 1.41-2(d) fraction) and (b) Subcomponent Identifier & Activity Nature (Active PoE Evaluation of Alternatives [§ 1.41-4(a)(5)] vs. Non-PoE Section 174A/174 Support vs. Excluded Post-Production/Routine Testing [§ 41(d)(4)] for the § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction).

Mandate Pre-Filing Subcomponent Hierarchy Mapping and Shrink-Back Modeling: To avoid the fatal "all-or-nothing" trap that resulted in a 100% credit disallowance in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), taxpayers must never track or define business components solely at the top-level commercial product, whole-vessel, or whole-platform level. Prior to return preparation, tax and engineering teams should map every development program into a documented parent-child hierarchy of discrete subcomponents (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B)) and compute the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) Process of Experimentation ratio at the parent level first (excluding any 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(d)(2) wage gross-ups). Whenever a parent business component falls below 80%—or sits dangerously close to the 80% cliff where an examiner's recharacterization of a few hours could disqualify the project—the taxpayer should proactively apply the Shrinking-Back Rule (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2)) in its pre-filing workpapers to isolate the specific experimental subsystems that clear the ≥80% PoE threshold with a defensible margin.

Substantiate Pilot-Model Production and Direct Supervision/Support Nexus Under Little Sandy Coal, Intermountain Electronics, and Moore: When including first-line supervisory wages (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2)), direct support wages (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(3)), or pilot-model fabrication labor (26 C.F.R. § 1.174-2(a)(4)) in the numerator of the business component 80% PoE fraction (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)), taxpayers must retain contemporaneous objective evidence demonstrating how those supervisory, support, or shop-floor fabrication activities were directly integrated into the evaluative process of testing alternatives to eliminate technical uncertainty. Furthermore, to survive scrutiny under Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20), organizational charts must verify that any supervisor claimed under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2) is an immediate first-line manager ("one-up") of researchers, while any hands-on research claimed for upper-tier executives is corroborated by contemporaneous engineering change orders, test protocols, CAD revision histories, Jira tickets, git commits, laboratory notebooks, and calendars.

Separate Physical Supply QREs from the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) Activity Fraction and Reconcile Section 174A Treatment: Because the Tax Court in Little Sandy Coal (T.C. Memo. 2021-15) held that physical supply expenditures (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C)) do not measure "activities" and must be excluded from both the numerator and the denominator of the 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction even under a cost-basis methodology, compliance workpapers must compute the ≥80% PoE ratio strictly across research activities (labor and activity costs) before adding eligible supply QREs to the qualified business component's credit pool. Finally, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, workpapers must verify that all research activities—including any ≤20% non-PoE research activities absorbed under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6)—are properly treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174A in accordance with amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and reconciled with the taxpayer's Section 280C(c) election.
